content:
Toph broke her ankle and immediately became the worst patient in the history of medicine.

“It is not broken.”

Katara’s hands glowed blue around the swelling.

“It is broken.”

“It’s annoyed.”

“Bones do not get annoyed.”

“Mine do.”

Aang stood in the clinic doorway trying not to smile.

I failed entirely.

Toph pointed at the sound of my laugh. “You. Traitor.”

“You tried to jump from a warehouse roof onto a moving cart.”

“I made it.”

“You landed sideways.”

“The cart moved wrong.”

“The cart was going in a straight line.”

“Suspicious.”

Katara looked up. “Do you want me to heal this or do you want to argue?”

“Both.”

“That was not an option.”

Toph crossed her arms.

The accident itself had been frightening.

A stolen shipment of blasting powder had led Toph and two city officers through the warehouse district. I had arrived just in time to see her leap from a roof, twist in the air, and come down with her left foot half on a cart rail.

The crack had been audible.

So had every word she yelled afterward.

Katara could accelerate healing, reduce swelling, and repair some of the damage. She could not make a serious fracture vanish in a single session without exhausting herself and risking poor healing.

Toph did not care for this information.

“How long?” she asked.

“Two weeks before you put full weight on it. Longer before you’re jumping off buildings.”

“No.”

Katara blinked. “That wasn’t a proposal.”

“I can’t see if I can’t use my feet.”

The room changed.

There it was.

Not stubbornness for sport.

Fear.

Toph’s seismic sense depended on contact with earth or connected solid surfaces. A splinted ankle did not make her helpless, but it disrupted the way she moved through the world.

Aang’s expression softened immediately.

Too immediately.

Toph heard it in his breath.

“Don’t.”

“I didn’t say anything.”

“You did the sad face.”

“You can’t see my face.”

“I can hear your sad face.”

I stepped beside the treatment table.

“Do you want help getting home?”

Toph turned toward me.

The question sat there.

Not Do you need help?

Not You can’t do this alone.

Do you want it?

Her shoulders lowered.

“Yeah.”

“Arm or chair?”

“Arm.”

Katara glanced at me, approval warm in her eyes.

Toph pointed at her. “Stop being proud.”

“I’m allowed.”

“No.”

Aang brought the crutches Katara had arranged.

Toph hated them on sight despite not seeing them.

“They squeak.”

“They’re temporary,” Aang said.

“So are you if you keep talking.”

Getting home took forty minutes.

Toph used one crutch and my forearm, testing every step. On packed earth she could still read vibration through her good foot. On wooden bridges, the information blurred. On a section of new metal walkway, she stopped.

I did not pull.

“What?” I asked.

“Too many echoes.”

“Want my arm tighter?”

“Yes.”

I shifted.

Toph’s hand closed around my sleeve.

We moved again.

A group of children recognized her near the market.

“The Blind Bandit!” one shouted.

Toph groaned.

A boy stared at the crutch. “Did somebody beat you?”

“Yeah,” Toph said. “A cart.”

The boy’s eyes widened.

“I’m getting a rematch.”

The children followed us for half a block asking whether carts could earthbend.

By the time we reached the house, Toph was laughing.

That helped.

The next morning did not.

I found her sitting on the front steps before sunrise, crutch beside her.

“You’re up early.”

“Couldn’t sleep.”

I sat without touching her.

Toph’s injured leg was propped on a cushion Katara had clearly placed there.

After a minute she said, “Everyone’s walking quieter.”

“What?”

“Aang. Katara. The students. They think I can’t tell.”

I listened.

Inside the house, Aang moved in the kitchen.

He was absolutely walking quieter.

“I can tell him to stop.”

Toph snorted. “He’ll apologize for ten minutes.”

“True.”

She rubbed her thumb along the edge of the step.

“I hate when people know I’m hurt.”

“I know.”

“No, you know I hate pity.”

“That too.”

Toph’s jaw tightened.

“When I was little, being hurt proved my parents right. If I fell, if I got sick, if I needed anything, it became evidence that I shouldn’t be allowed out of the house.”

I waited.

“So I got good at not needing.”

The sentence was simple.

The years behind it were not.

I leaned my shoulder against hers.

“Needing something now doesn’t rewrite what you were capable of then.”

Toph was quiet.

“And accepting help doesn’t mean the person helping gets authority over you.”

“Yeah.”

“You taught me that.”

She turned her face toward me.

“Annoying when I’m smart, huh?”

“Devastating.”

Aang came out carrying breakfast.

He stopped when he saw us.

Toph pointed toward him. “Walk normal.”

Aang froze.

“I am walking normal.”

“You’re sneaking around like a lemur with a secret.”

“I was trying not to wake you.”

“I was awake.”

“I know that now.”

“Also stop looking sad.”

Aang’s mouth opened.

I cut in. “She can hear your sad face.”

Toph slapped my arm in approval.

Aang sat on the other side of her.

“Okay,” he said. “What do you want from me?”

Toph considered.

“Breakfast.”

He handed her a bowl.

“And?”

“Treat me normal.”

Aang nodded.

Then he stole a dumpling from her bowl.

Toph punched him in the ribs.

“Too normal!”

Katara opened the door behind us. “If either of you damages that ankle again, I’m freezing both of you to the porch.”

Toph grinned.

I looked at the three of them and felt the shape of care become clearer.

Aang cared by adapting.

Katara cared by protecting recovery.

I cared by asking what Toph wanted instead of deciding.

Toph cared by trusting us enough to answer.

For the next two weeks, she complained constantly.

She also accepted an arm when she wanted one.

She used a cane when the crutch became unnecessary.

She taught classes seated, terrifying students with thrown pebbles whenever their stances were lazy.

And on the first day Katara cleared her to stand fully, Toph planted both feet on the courtyard earth and closed her eyes.

The relief on her face was so naked that none of us spoke.

The city returned to her through the ground.

Carts. Footsteps. Pipes. Hammers. Heartbeats.

Toph breathed in.

Then she grinned.

“Okay,” she said. “Which one of you wants to fight?”

Aang stepped backward.

Katara pointed at me.

I stared at her.

Toph cracked her knuckles.

Love, apparently, had limits.

Toph’s hatred of pity became easier to understand when strangers visited.

One council aide arrived with flowers, lowered his voice as if entering a funeral, and asked Toph whether she was “managing bravely.”

Toph stared at him from the couch.

“I broke an ankle.”

“Yes, of course, but for someone in your condition—”

Katara inhaled sharply.

I stepped between them before either woman committed a felony.

“Her condition is that she has a broken ankle.”

The aide blinked. “I only meant—”

“I know.”

Toph’s face had gone very still.

The man left five minutes later with his flowers and several new opinions about our household.

Toph waited until the door shut.

“Could’ve handled him.”

“I know.”

“You stepped in anyway.”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

I considered the question.

“Because you shouldn’t have to spend energy proving you’re a person every time somebody decides to be stupid.”

Her jaw moved once.

Katara returned with tea and set it down without fuss.

Aang placed the crutches within easy reach, not in her hands.

Nobody praised her for enduring anything.

That evening, Toph asked me to help carry a stack of academy papers upstairs.

It was the first time since the injury she had asked for help before attempting the task herself.

I picked them up without comment.

Halfway up, she said, “This doesn’t mean anything.”

“Obviously.”

“I still hate needing people.”

“You can hate it.”

She was quiet.

Then: “You’re not terrible at this.”

From Toph, it was practically a love letter.

Two days later, Toph asked Aang to walk with her to the academy. She could have gone alone. He understood the significance well enough not to mention it.

When they returned, she was carrying her own crutches under one arm and insulting his posture.

Katara glanced at me.

Neither of us smiled until Toph had gone upstairs.

Then Katara whispered, “Progress.”

From above, Toph shouted, “I heard that!”

“Of course you did,” I called back.

The answer was a thump against the floorboards and, unmistakably, a laugh.

When the cast finally came off, Toph stood without moving for a long moment, feeling the full floor through both feet again. None of us cheered.

She inhaled, stamped once, and a ring of pebbles jumped around her ankles.

Then she grinned.

Aang grinned back. Katara folded her arms, pretending she had not been waiting for exactly that sound.

I said, “No walls.”

Toph’s grin widened. “No promises.”

Toph took three steps, then five, then crossed the room without help. We watched without hovering. That was harder than it sounded.
